groundTruthKeyFormat: { sourceTitle, page, snippet } — snippet is a ~70 char prefix of the unit text. Content-derived, so it is stable across reseeds where Mongo ObjectIds are not.
limitations: The seeded course contains no figures or diagrams, so there are no true figure-based questions. Questions tagged 'structure' ask about a structure described in prose (e.g. the virtual-address bit split), which is the closest honest analogue.
Single synthetic course written by us. Every question is therefore written by the same authors who wrote the material, which biases toward in-material questions.
Off-material questions are authored by the same team, so their difficulty distribution is not necessarily representative of real student questions.

entries.question: What problem does virtual memory solve that a physical address space cannot?
entries.referenceAnswer: It reconciles each process's need for a contiguous address space with fragmented, finite physical memory, providing isolation between processes, the illusion of a large contiguous space, and the ability to run programs larger than physical RAM.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Every process sees its own contiguous address space

entries.question: Why do modern systems use multi-level page tables instead of one flat table?
entries.referenceAnswer: A flat page table is too large to keep resident, so systems use multiple levels; with a four-level table on x86-64, three levels are only allocated when actually used, so programs with a small working set pay a very small translation cost.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: The page table itself is usually too large to keep resident

entries.question: What is the role of the TLB and why does it matter so much for pointer-chasing code?
entries.referenceAnswer: The TLB is a small fully-associative cache in the MMU holding recent virtual-to-physical translations. A TLB hit avoids the page table walk entirely, which is the single largest performance factor in pointer-chasing code; a miss costs roughly an order of magnitude more than a cache hit.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small fully-associative cache

entries.question: How does the Clock replacement algorithm avoid evicting pages that are still in active use?
entries.referenceAnswer: It keeps a reference bit on each frame. On eviction the hand clears the reference bit and moves on; only a frame whose bit was already clear is actually evicted.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: The Clock or Second Chance algorithm approximates LRU

entries.question: Why does the course say set-associativity is the practical compromise for caches?
entries.referenceAnswer: Direct-mapped caches are fast but suffer conflict misses when two hot addresses map to the same set; fully associative caches avoid conflict misses but need a full associativity search on every lookup, which is impractical for large caches. Set-associative confines replacement to a few ways, raising hit rate while keeping the hardware search parallel and cheap.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Set-associative caching is the practical compromise

entries.question: What formally defines a data race in this lecture?
entries.referenceAnswer: Two threads access the same memory location concurrently, at least one access is a write, and there is no ordering between them.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location

entries.question: Why should a mutex protect the smallest possible critical section?
entries.referenceAnswer: Because under contention the cost of acquiring a mutex rises sharply, so a larger critical section serialises threads for longer.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A mutex provides mutual exclusion

entries.question: What two locality properties does the cache hierarchy exploit?
entries.referenceAnswer: Locality in time (recently accessed addresses are likely to be accessed again) and locality in space (addresses near a recent access are also likely).

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Memory is organised as a hierarchy of caches

entries.question: How does breaking a global lock ordering prevent deadlock?
entries.referenceAnswer: Imposing a global lock ordering breaks circular wait by construction, and since deadlock requires all four conditions simultaneously, eliminating one eliminates the deadlock.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Deadlock requires four conditions to hold simultaneously

entries.question: Why is a data race described as a source of difficult concurrency bugs?
entries.referenceAnswer: Because the observed behaviour is not reproducible.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: are the source of most difficult concurrency bugs

entries.question: When is a reader-writer lock a bad choice?
entries.referenceAnswer: When writes are frequent, because the extra bookkeeping can make it slower than a plain mutex.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A reader-writer lock allows many concurrent readers

entries.question: What makes atomic operations tricky to use correctly across different architectures?
entries.referenceAnswer: They require careful memory ordering to be correct across architectures. Sequential consistency is easiest to reason about but most expensive; relaxed ordering is fastest but requires explicit fences where ordering actually matters.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: An atomic operation provides per-location mutual exclusion without a lock

entries.question: How do I keep a program that is bigger than the machine's RAM from failing?
entries.referenceAnswer: Virtual memory provides the ability to run programs larger than physical RAM by giving each process the illusion of a large contiguous space.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Every process sees its own contiguous address space

entries.question: Why do pointer-heavy loops suffer more than arithmetic-heavy ones?
entries.referenceAnswer: A TLB miss costs roughly an order of magnitude more than a cache hit and the TLB hit avoids the page table walk, so working-set size matters more than raw instruction count in memory-bound workloads.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small fully-associative cache

entries.question: What should I reach for when scanning a large array kills my cache performance?
entries.referenceAnswer: Cache line size trades transfer bandwidth against waste: larger lines help sequential workloads by amortising the tag lookup.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Cache line size trades transfer bandwidth against waste

entries.question: My program keeps getting OOM-killed even though memory looks free. Why?
entries.referenceAnswer: Strict LRU suffers badly from sequential scans that evict the entire working set and then immediately reload it; this thrashing pathology is why Linux moved away from strict LRU.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: LRU evicts the least recently used page

entries.question: Why did nobody implement a fully associative cache for main memory?
entries.referenceAnswer: Fully associative caches avoid conflict misses entirely but need a full associativity search on every lookup, which is why they are impractical for large caches.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Direct-mapped caches map each block to exactly one location

entries.question: What is the cheapest way to stop two threads clobbering a shared counter?
entries.referenceAnswer: A mutex provides mutual exclusion: only one thread may hold the lock at a time, so the critical section is serialised.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A mutex provides mutual exclusion

entries.question: How do I know if a bug is a race rather than ordinary logic error?
entries.referenceAnswer: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location concurrently and at least one access is a write with no ordering between them; such bugs are not reproducible.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A data race occurs when two threads access the same memory location

entries.question: Why does my swap-heavy machine slow to a crawl on a small working set?
entries.referenceAnswer: Programs with a small working set should pay a very small translation cost with multi-level page tables; degradation like this points at thrashing from strict-LRU-style sequential-scan eviction.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: The page table itself is usually too large to keep resident

entries.question: Should I take the strongest memory ordering available?
entries.referenceAnswer: No. Sequential consistency is the easiest model to reason about but is the most expensive; relaxed ordering is fastest but requires explicit fences where ordering actually matters.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: An atomic operation provides per-location mutual exclusion without a lock

entries.question: What are the symptoms of a deadlock and how do I rule it out?
entries.referenceAnswer: Deadlock requires mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait simultaneously; breaking any one eliminates it.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Deadlock requires four conditions to hold simultaneously

entries.question: What is the cost model for grabbing a lock when nothing else is competing?
entries.referenceAnswer: Two atomic operations in the uncontended case, on the order of twenty nanoseconds.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A mutex provides mutual exclusion

entries.question: How do page faults differ depending on whether the data is already in RAM?
entries.referenceAnswer: A minor fault means the page is present in memory but the mapping is not yet established; a major fault means the page is not in memory at all and must be read from the backing store, costing a disk or SSD access.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A page fault occurs when a translation is not valid in the page table

entries.question: Trace what the MMU does with a 48-bit virtual address on a 4 KiB page system, and say which component makes the step cheap.
entries.referenceAnswer: The low 12 bits are the page offset and the upper 36 bits are the virtual page number; the MMU consults the page table to translate the virtual page number into a physical frame number, then concatenates the frame number with the offset. The TLB makes this cheap by caching recent translations and avoiding the page table walk.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Every process sees its own contiguous address space
The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small fully-associative cache

entries.question: Explain why strict LRU fails on sequential scans and what the lecture proposes instead.
entries.referenceAnswer: LRU evicts the least recently used page and is cheap to approximate with a clock hand, but it suffers badly from sequential scans that evict the entire working set and then immediately reload it; this thrashing pathology is why Linux moved away from strict LRU. The Clock or Second Chance algorithm approximates LRU with a reference bit: the hand clears the bit and moves on, and only a frame whose bit was already clear is evicted.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: LRU evicts the least recently used page
The Clock or Second Chance algorithm approximates LRU

entries.question: Compare direct-mapped, fully associative and set-associative caches in terms of conflict misses and lookup cost.
entries.referenceAnswer: Direct-mapped caches map each block to one location: fast and simple but suffer conflict misses when two hot addresses map to the same set. Fully associative caches avoid conflict misses but need a full associativity search per lookup, impractical for large caches. Set-associative is the practical compromise: a 4-way set has 4 candidate locations, replacement is confined to those ways, and the search stays parallel and cheap.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Direct-mapped caches map each block to exactly one location
Set-associative caching is the practical compromise

entries.question: Why does a mutex sometimes lose to a reader-writer lock and sometimes beat it?
entries.referenceAnswer: A mutex serialises the critical section with acquisition costing two atomic operations uncontended (~20ns) but rising sharply under contention. A reader-writer lock lets many readers run concurrently, helping when reads dominate and the critical section is long, but the extra bookkeeping makes it slower than a plain mutex when writes are frequent.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A mutex provides mutual exclusion
A reader-writer lock allows many concurrent readers

entries.question: How do the guarantees of virtual memory and the performance of the TLB relate to each other?
entries.referenceAnswer: Virtual memory provides isolation, the illusion of a large contiguous space, and running programs larger than RAM, implemented with multi-level page tables so a small working set pays little translation cost. The TLB accelerates this by avoiding the page table walk, which is the single largest performance factor in pointer-chasing code.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Every process sees its own contiguous address space
The TLB (translation lookaside buffer) is a small fully-associative cache

entries.question: Describe the trade-off between cache line size and access pattern.
entries.referenceAnswer: Cache line size trades transfer bandwidth against waste. A 64-byte line on a 64-byte-aligned address means an aligned 8-byte load pulls in 64 bytes, of which 56 are wasted. Larger lines help sequential workloads by amortising the tag lookup; smaller lines help random pointer chasing by reducing waste.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Cache line size trades transfer bandwidth against waste

entries.question: How does the lecture's definition of deadlock interact with the lock-ordering technique?
entries.referenceAnswer: Deadlock needs all four conditions simultaneously — mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait — so breaking any one eliminates it. A global lock ordering breaks circular wait by construction and is the most common practical technique.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: Deadlock requires four conditions to hold simultaneously

entries.referenceAnswer: A minor fault means the page is present in memory but the mapping is not established, e.g. after fork; a major fault means the page is not in memory and must be read from backing store, costing a disk or SSD access. Programs larger than physical RAM depend on major faults being served from backing store.

groundTruthUnits.snippet: A page fault occurs when a translation is not valid in the page table

entries.question: Compare a mutex with a reader-writer lock in terms of when each is the right choice.
entries.referenceAnswer: A mutex serialises the critical section and is the simplest option. A reader-writer lock allows many concurrent readers but only a single writer, helping when reads dominate writes and the critical section is long; it can hurt when writes are frequent because the extra bookkeeping can make it slower than a plain mutex.

entries.referenceAnswer: A flat page table is usually too large to keep resident. Multi-level page tables allocate upper levels only when used, so a four-level table on x86-64 means three levels are only allocated when actually used and small-working-set programs pay a very small translation cost.
